directions.hypothesis: In larger genomes, the extra prophage-associated gene clusters are mostly core within their species, which suggests domesticated remnants, whereas in smaller genomes they are mostly accessory or single-genome.
directions.outcomes: Support: the size-linked increase is concentrated in core prophage-derived clusters, and dedicated detection finds little more intact prophage in large genomes. Refute: the increase is in accessory or single-genome clusters and tracks intact prophage calls, favouring active carriage.
directions.prior_work: PMID 25092302 showed that bacteria domesticate defective prophages, and PMID 28692019 related phage evolution to host and genome features; neither asks whether genome size predicts prophage-module content across the pangenome through domesticated core clusters.
directions.question: Does the strong link between genome size and prophage-module content arise because larger genomes retain domesticated, species-wide prophage-derived genes, rather than carrying more recently acquired intact prophages?
directions.readiness_basis: The pangenome, annotation and genome-size tables are in the catalog; dedicated prophage calls on a subset would have to be generated.
directions.test: For species in the pangenome, tally prophage-associated gene clusters by module and by whether the cluster is core, accessory or single-genome in its species. Relate each class to genome size within genera, and compare with non-prophage accessory genes to see whether prophage content scales differently. In a subset, call prophages with a dedicated detector and compare intact calls with annotation-based counts.
directions.title: Are large bacterial genomes rich in prophage modules because those modules become domesticated?
directions.why_it_matters: Genome size predicted prophage-module composition far more than environment or family-level phylogeny. The annotation-based method counts domesticated remnants as well as intact prophages, so it cannot say what the size effect means. Separating domestication from active carriage would show whether genome size reflects genome-wide tolerance of mobile DNA or long-term retention of useful phage-derived functions.

directions.hypothesis: SNIPE-family hosts carry ManYZ-type transporters more often than relatedness predicts, and deleting manYZ in a SNIPE-carrying strain changes its phage susceptibility.
directions.outcomes: Support: co-occurrence exceeds lineage expectation and manYZ loss shifts phage susceptibility in the SNIPE strain. Refute: co-occurrence matches relatedness and the deletion leaves infection unchanged.
directions.prior_work: PMID 41741653 shows a membrane-bound nuclease cleaving phage DNA during injection and PMID 34032565 shows membrane defenses and counter-defenses in E. coli; neither tests co-occurrence across species or the role of ManYZ in Klebsiella.
directions.question: Do species carrying SNIPE-family DUF4041 proteins also carry ManYZ-type transporters more often than expected from relatedness, and does a SNIPE host's susceptibility to phages depend on its ManYZ?
directions.readiness_basis: Co-occurrence and E. coli susceptibility analyses use catalog tables, but Klebsiella-specific fitness was unmeasured and deletion mutants in SNIPE-carrying strains must be built.
directions.test: Across the pangenome, test co-occurrence of DUF4041 clusters, restricted to those with additional SNIPE-family features where available, with ManYZ-type transporter clusters within genera. In E. coli, where phage susceptibility calls exist, ask whether strains with SNIPE and ManYZ differ in susceptibility from strains lacking either. In Klebsiella, where the catalog shows annotations but no fitness data, build deletion mutants of manYZ in a SNIPE-carrying strain such as NCTC9140 or HS11286 and challenge them with phages.
directions.title: Is the SNIPE phage-defense nuclease tied to hosts that carry the ManYZ phage-entry transporter?
directions.why_it_matters: The DUF4041 domain was found in 4,572 gene clusters across 1,696 species, but an estimated 80.4% of clusters are SNIPE-family proteins, so the rest may be other proteins or annotation noise. A link between a defense and the host entry route it guards would show how defenses coevolve with the proteins phages exploit and would help predict which strains phage therapy can reach.

directions.hypothesis: Tolerance phenotypes depend on gene copy number or regulatory variants of resistance genes rather than their presence, so adding copy number and promoter variants for efflux and detoxification genes will improve prediction for these conditions where presence alone fails.
directions.outcomes: Support: dosage and regulatory features raise held-out prediction for metals and antibiotics while leaving presence-only models unimproved. Refute: prediction stays poor with these features, pointing to unmeasured factors such as plasmids or physiology.
directions.question: Why can growth on amino acids, nucleosides and some carbon sources be predicted from the presence of gene families, while metal, antibiotic and nitrogen conditions cannot?
directions.readiness_basis: The existing genome-to-growth corpus lacks graded-dose tolerance measurements and copy-number or promoter-variant data, so these must be measured.
directions.test: Choose a panel of strains from the Oak Ridge isolate collection spanning several genera, and measure growth with graded doses of several metals and antibiotics. Sequence them to determine copy number and promoter variants of known resistance and efflux genes. Compare models using presence alone with models adding copy number and promoter variants, holding out whole genera.
directions.title: Is metal and antibiotic tolerance unpredictable from gene content because of gene dosage?
directions.why_it_matters: If tolerance depends on dosage and regulation, genome-based prediction of resistance and metal tolerance needs different features than metabolic growth prediction, and presence-based surveys of resistance genes will mislead.

directions.hypothesis: Warming-enriched genera carry the glyoxylate-cycle genes and other traits of fast-growing opportunists more often than warming-depleted genera. This would make the weak, uncorrected glyoxylate-gene signals a trait of the winners rather than noise.
directions.outcomes: Support: winners carry the glyoxylate-cycle genes more often and respond more strongly to the acetate pulse in heated soil. Refutation: winners and losers do not differ in these traits, or the carbon pulse favors both groups equally. The original shifts came from one sampling date, and the organic-horizon samples were all lab-incubated, so a refutation could also mean those shifts do not recur.
directions.prior_work: PMID 25762989 reports individual Actinobacteria and Acidobacteria members responding to Harvard Forest warming, and PMID 34512564 and 40105318 describe warming-responsive transcripts and pangenome changes. None compares genome traits of rising and falling taxa or tests them with a carbon pulse.
directions.question: In Harvard Forest organic soil, Actinobacteria rose and Acidobacteria fell under long-term warming. Do the genera that rise share genome traits, such as the glyoxylate cycle and larger genomes, that the falling genera lack?
directions.readiness_basis: The catalog lists taxonomic profile, gene annotation and genome bin tables, but whether Harvard Forest bins are present was not shown, and the activity test needs new heated and control cores.
directions.test: Step 1 (analysis): list the genera that rose or fell in the heated plots from the taxonomic profiles. Find genome bins from matching soils and compare winners with losers for the glyoxylate-cycle genes, genome size and annotated carbon-cycling gene content, using related species in the pangenome collection as a cross-check. Step 2 (experiment): in fresh heated and control cores from the same plots, add a labile carbon source such as acetate. Measure respiration and use quantitative PCR to follow the winner and loser groups.
directions.title: Does long-term warming favor soil bacteria that carry fast-growth and glyoxylate-cycle traits?
directions.why_it_matters: It would turn a phylum-level shift seen at one time point into a trait-based prediction of which soil bacteria gain under warming. That would inform models of warmed forest carbon, which currently treat the community as a block.

directions.hypothesis: For lung-adapted, toxin-type-matched isolates, metabolic overlap weighted by the isolate's own substrate preferences predicts commensal inhibition better than overlap weighted by the laboratory strain's preferences, with amino acids carrying most of the signal.
directions.outcomes: Support: strain-specific weighting predicts inhibition clearly better, and amino acids carry the predictive signal. Refutation: laboratory-strain weighting predicts as well, or inhibition of lung isolates is unrelated to overlap. That would point to non-metabolic inhibition mechanisms.
directions.prior_work: PMID 17873029 describes carbon preferences of Pseudomonas in cystic fibrosis sputum and PMID 27881418 shows environmental pseudomonads inhibiting patient-derived isolates. Neither tests whether strain-specific substrate weighting predicts inhibition of lung-adapted isolates.
directions.question: The cystic fibrosis formulation work measured inhibition only on a laboratory strain that carries a different toxin type from most cystic fibrosis isolates, and no sugar or amino acid gave commensals a clear edge. Does inhibition of lung isolates depend on overlap in amino acid use instead?
directions.readiness_basis: Existing competition and virulence tables supply the commensal panel and typing, but inhibition and substrate preferences for toxin-type-matched lung isolates have not been measured; their column contents were not shown.
directions.test: Choose commensals from the existing competition screen and a panel of ExoS-positive cystic fibrosis isolates plus the laboratory strain. Measure growth inhibition of each isolate in co-culture and in conditioned medium. Measure each isolate's growth on sugars and amino acids directly, so any sugar-use difference is observed rather than inferred from pathway scores. Compute overlap weighted by each isolate's measured substrate preferences. Compare how well strain-specific and laboratory-strain weighting predict inhibition, and repeat with the three-member formulation that adds Micrococcus luteus.
directions.title: Do commensals inhibit lung-adapted Pseudomonas by competing for amino acids rather than sugars?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether formulations designed around one reference strain transfer to the strains in patients. Lung isolates score lower on several sugar pathways, which the earlier work reads as possible metabolic streamlining (an interpretation, not a measured loss), so the test also shows whether design should target amino acid use.

directions.hypothesis: Within Pseudomonas fluorescens-group and P. putida species, plant-root isolates grow faster than water isolates on xylose, arabinose and myo-inositol. The pathway genes are present in both, so the difference lies in transport or regulation that pathway-presence calls cannot see.
directions.outcomes: Support: growth rates differ by habitat on these sugars among isolates with identical pathway calls, and fast and slow growers differ in transporter or regulator variants. Refutation: rates are similar across habitats, or they track pathway completeness only. The coarse-pathway explanation for the weak habitat signal would then fall away.
directions.prior_work: PMID 22576821 links substrate-use profiles of 23 Pseudomonas strains to rhizosphere competence, and PMID 41332517 reports strain-level metabolic variation within P. putida. Neither compares growth rates among isolates of one species with identical pathway content across habitats.
directions.question: Pathway presence alone discriminated habitats only modestly among free-living Pseudomonas. Do isolates of one species from soil, plant roots and water differ in growth rate on plant-derived sugars even when the same pathway is present in all of them?
directions.readiness_basis: Pathway calls and isolation metadata are in the catalog, but growth rates of habitat-sorted isolates on these sugars must be measured, and how many species have enough isolates per habitat was not shown.
directions.test: From the pangenome collection, choose species with isolates from at least two habitats whose genomes all carry the three pathways. Order or obtain about 10 isolates per habitat. Measure growth rate and yield on each sugar as sole carbon source in plate readers. Compare habitats within species. Check whether growth tracks the pathway-completeness scores, and compare with carbon-source growth in the Putida mutant-fitness experiments and in the strain-level utilization records for the same species. Then compare sugar-transporter and regulator gene variants between fast and slow growers.
directions.title: Do Pseudomonas from different habitats differ in how fast they use plant sugars despite equal pathways?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that habitat adaptation in carbon use sits in quantitative performance, not gene presence. That would explain the weak habitat signal in pathway profiles, and it would redirect the search for niche markers toward regulation and transport variants.

directions.hypothesis: The host-specific subclades of both species carry gains concentrated in secretion-system and effector functions, not metabolic functions. Moving the subclade-specific effector set into a strain from another subclade shifts its ability to colonize the matching host.
directions.outcomes: Support: both specializations are enriched for secretion and effector functions, and the transfer shifts host colonization toward the matching plant. Refutation: the subclade-specific gene sets are unrelated in function between the two species, or the transfer does not change host outcome. Host range would then depend on genes outside these clusters. Only 18 of 65 plant-associated species had tree data, so the pattern may not generalize beyond these two.
directions.prior_work: PMID 35536128 relates X. campestris pathovar to genomic relatedness and host range, and PMID 32040377 reports gene content enriched in corn-infecting X. vasicola. Neither compares the two host specializations for functional convergence or tests the subclade-specific genes by transfer.
directions.question: Two Xanthomonas species each split into subclades that segregate by plant host: X. campestris with Brassica and X. vasicola with maize. Did these two specializations arise by gaining the same kind of accessory genes, or by unrelated changes?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene-cluster, annotation and tree tables are listed, but the subclade-specific gene sets must be computed and the transfer test needs new plant assays; whether trees exist for these two species was not shown.
directions.test: Step 1 (analysis): in the subclades already identified, extract gene families present in the host-matched subclade and absent from the others. Classify them by function and compare the two species for convergence. Step 2 (experiment): clone the top subclade-specific effector or secretion cluster into a strain from a non-matching subclade of the same species. Test colonization and symptoms on Brassica and maize.
directions.title: Is host specialization in Xanthomonas carried by a small shared set of accessory genes?
directions.why_it_matters: A shared functional class would suggest a general route by which plant pathogens specialize, and would give a short list of genes for surveillance of emerging pathovars. Unrelated changes would mean host range cannot be predicted from gene class.

directions.hypothesis: Human-associated genomes carry more intact prophage per megabase than soil or marine genomes, and their anti-defense genes sit inside those intact elements. If the enrichment is mostly remnants, the intact density will not differ between habitats.
directions.outcomes: Support: intact prophage density is higher in human-associated genomes, anti-defense genes sit within them, and some isolates release virions. Refutation: intact density is similar across habitats and the enriched genes lie outside intact elements, which would favor domesticated remnants. Habitat sampling is uneven in the collection, and defense-table contents were not shown.
directions.prior_work: PMID 25092302 shows pervasive domestication of defective prophages, and PMID 40639337 describes phage counter-defense repertoires. Neither compares intact prophage density across habitats or places habitat-enriched anti-defense genes inside intact elements.
directions.question: Tail, head and anti-defense gene groups of prophages are more common in human-associated species, yet no single phage lineage tracked environment. Are these genes part of intact, potentially inducible prophages, or are they remnants kept by the host?
directions.readiness_basis: Mobile-element and defense tables by habitat are listed, but per-genome normalization and overlap with gene groups must be computed, and the induction assays need new measurements.
directions.test: Use the mobile-element calls and defense annotations for the genome collection grouped by habitat. Count intact prophage and phage-type elements per megabase in human gut, soil and marine genomes, and check whether anti-defense and tail genes lie inside them. Compare the same genomes with the earlier annotation-based module counts. Follow with induction assays on a few human-gut isolates that carry the elements, to see whether virions are released.
directions.title: Are phage tail and anti-defense genes enriched in human-associated bacteria carried by intact prophages?
directions.why_it_matters: Intact prophages are a live source of gene transfer and host killing, while remnants are inert baggage. Telling them apart decides whether the human-associated pattern reflects ongoing phage-host conflict or past events that cost nothing now.

directions.hypothesis: Truly dark genes with strong nutrient phenotypes are co-fit with annotated transporters or catabolic genes for the same substrate more often than annotation-lag genes with nutrient phenotypes are. Their stress phenotypes show no such substrate-matched partners.
directions.outcomes: Support: substrate-matched partners are clearly more common for truly dark nutrient genes than for annotation-lag nutrient genes, in several organisms. Refute: partners are no more substrate-matched than for annotation-lag genes, or the effect lives only in one or two organisms.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29769716 and PMID 22125499 tie poorly annotated genes to conditions but do not contrast truly dark genes with annotation-lag genes or test whether co-fit partners match the substrate.
directions.question: Genes still uncharacterized after modern reannotation were less common in stress conditions than annotation-lag genes (28.7% versus 43.2%) and more common in nutrient, mixed-community and iron conditions. Is that nutrient signal a real, substrate-specific function, or a by-product of how conditions were sampled?
directions.readiness_basis: Condition-class, gene and annotation tables for the 48 organisms are in the catalog; the co-fitness partner step and the substrate matching need new code, and the catalog did not show the co-fitness table's columns.
directions.test: In the transposon-fitness compendium for 48 bacteria, define strong-phenotype truly dark genes and annotation-lag genes with one fixed definition of strong phenotype and of condition class, and record the resulting stress shares for both gene classes, since the two reported pairs differ (28.7% versus 43.2% in one comparison, 43.3% versus 54.7% in another). For each gene, find its most co-fit partners and the single carbon or nitrogen source behind its strongest phenotype. Ask whether the partners carry transporter or catabolic annotations for that same compound. Compare the two gene classes within each organism so that condition coverage is matched. Add a check that excludes the two Methanococcus strains, which hold most truly dark genes.
directions.title: Do truly dark genes with nutrient phenotypes encode unrecognized substrate-specific transport or catabolic steps?
directions.why_it_matters: It would turn a vague nutrient enrichment into concrete function predictions for the least-annotated genes. It would also show whether 'stress response' is the wrong default frame for ranking dark genes for experiments.

directions.hypothesis: Most shallow-alignment core clusters are restricted to a single genus or family, which points to recent origin. Shallow clusters with relatives spread across many phyla are a minority.
directions.outcomes: Support: the large majority of shallow core clusters are confined to one genus or family, far more than the matched deep clusters, and this persists in the balanced sample. Refute: most have relatives across many phyla, which favors divergence over recent origin, or the confinement disappears once sampling is balanced.
directions.prior_work: PMID 41273079 and PMID 34791371 describe structure-database coverage, and PMID 37821698 surveys functional dark matter in metagenomes. None asks whether conserved low-depth proteins are lineage-restricted or ancient.
directions.question: Hundreds of thousands of core gene clusters have very shallow multiple-sequence-alignment depth (few related sequences found when AlphaFold's alignments were built), and most are hypothetical. Does shallowness mean recent, lineage-restricted origin, or ancient families that diverged beyond recognition?
directions.readiness_basis: Cluster, annotation, taxonomy and alignment-depth tables are in the catalog but are very large; the cross-clade family counts and the balanced sampling have to be computed.
directions.test: Take core clusters whose representative sequence has a very shallow alignment depth. For each, use protein-family identifiers from the annotation tables to count how many species clades and phyla hold a related cluster. Compare against core clusters with deep alignments and against accessory clusters, matched for protein length. The genome collection is not phylogenetically balanced (Pseudomonas and E. coli are over-represented), so repeat the comparison on a sample balanced across genera and phyla, and judge lineage restriction only on counts that survive it. Alignment depth was looked up for the representative sequence only, so also check a few members per cluster. Finally, ask whether clusters confined to one lineage are the ones with essential or condition-specific phenotypes in the transposon-fitness compendium.
directions.title: Are conserved core proteins with shallow sequence alignments young lineage inventions or ancient divergent families?
directions.why_it_matters: The two readings predict different work. Lineage-restricted proteins call for ecology and de novo gene-origin studies. Divergent ancient families call for structure-based function recovery.

directions.hypothesis: Within genera that contain both carriers and non-carriers, carriers come from more variable environments than their non-carrying relatives. Their gene copy is more often accessory than core.
directions.outcomes: Support: carriers are consistently more variable-habitat within genera, beyond genome size, with accessory-gene copies. Refute: within-genus differences vanish or point the other way, so the global pattern is lineage inheritance.
directions.prior_work: PMID 17113245 and PMID 24887088 infer horizontal transfer of PHA genes from individual phylogenies, and PMID 42203387 links PHA to fluctuating environments. None tests habitat variability among carriers and non-carriers inside the same genus.
directions.question: Species from highly variable environments carry the PHB synthase gene more often than species from stable ones, in every genome-size band. Does that reflect selection after repeated horizontal acquisition into variable-habitat lineages, rather than inheritance from a PHB-carrying ancestor?
directions.readiness_basis: Annotations, taxonomy and environmental embeddings are in the catalog, but embeddings cover only a minority of genomes, so power per genus must be computed.
directions.test: Identify genera with both PHB-synthase-positive and negative species. For each group, compare habitat variability, from the spread of environmental embeddings over genomes with coordinates, and genome size. Test whether carriers sit in more variable habitats than relatives. Check whether the gene copy is accessory in carriers from variable habitats.
directions.title: Is the link between polyhydroxybutyrate genes and variable habitats caused by repeated gene gain?
directions.why_it_matters: Ancestry and genome size are the two standing confounds of the feast-and-famine storage idea. A within-genus contrast removes most ancestry effects and would show whether variable habitats select for storage gain.

directions.hypothesis: The dark genes of Methanococcus have strong co-fitness partners enriched for annotated methanogenesis, cofactor and nutrient-utilization genes. The partners are concentrated in a small number of coherent groups, not scattered at random.
directions.outcomes: Support: partner enrichment for methanogenesis or cofactor functions, with the dark genes falling into a few modules shared by both strains. Refute: partners are no more functional than random and modules are not shared between strains.
directions.prior_work: PMID 39120137 maps nutrient and energy-metabolism genes in a model methanogen by high-throughput genetics. It does not ask what the genes that remain unannotated after reannotation are doing.
directions.question: Two Methanococcus strains hold more than half of all truly dark genes. Are these genes functionally coherent archaeal biology that annotation databases lack, or an unstructured collection?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness tables for both strains are in the catalog; the module grouping and cross-archaea family lookup need new computation.
directions.test: Using the transposon-fitness compendium, collect the dark genes of the two Methanococcus strains and their co-fit partners. Test whether the partners are enriched for annotated methanogenesis and cofactor functions beyond a gene-length-matched random set. Check whether the same dark genes are conserved in the other Methanococcus strain and in other archaea, using the protein-cluster resources. Group dark genes by shared partners to get testable modules.
directions.title: Do the unannotated genes of Methanococcus belong to methanogen-specific energy and cofactor metabolism?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, a small set of archaeal-specific functions explains much of the remaining dark gene space. Targeted methanogen work would then be a more efficient route to it than broad surveys.

directions.hypothesis: Slowing quinate catabolism removes the Complex I requirement, and raising alternative NADH dehydrogenase capacity relieves it. Complex I essentiality follows the rate of NADH production, not its yield.
directions.outcomes: Support: the Complex I growth defect shrinks as quinate supply slows and recovers when the alternative enzyme is overexpressed, with a higher NADH ratio in the deletion on fast quinate. Refute: the defect stays equally severe at every supply rate and overexpression does not rescue it.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18319726 and PMID 25374488 describe ADP1 growth and expression on quinate. Neither examines Complex I need as a function of NADH production rate.
directions.question: Quinate yields less NADH per carbon than glucose or acetate, yet Complex I is more essential on quinate. Does a fast burst of NADH from ring cleavage exceed the capacity of the alternative enzyme?
directions.readiness_basis: The central prediction needs growth and NADH measurements under controlled supply rates that are not in the catalog, and the alternative enzyme has no growth data.
directions.test: In Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1, grow Complex I deletion and wild-type strains on quinate at several limiting supply rates and on quinate mixed with a slowly used carbon. Measure growth and the NADH to NAD+ ratio. Repeat with the alternative NADH dehydrogenase overexpressed. Compare with the same strains on glucose and acetate.
directions.title: Does Complex I matter on quinate because ring cleavage overloads the alternative NADH dehydrogenase?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that respiratory wiring is set by flux dynamics, not by pathway stoichiometry. That would explain why alternative-enzyme presence did not predict Complex I dispensability across species.

directions.hypothesis: Lipid A loss is tolerated only if the cbb3 and related respiratory operon stays active. Deleting it in the rescued strain removes viability even though sphingolipid levels are unchanged.
directions.outcomes: Support: loss of the respiratory operon makes the rescued strain inviable with sphingolipid levels unchanged, and low oxygen worsens it. Refute: the strain stays viable without the operon, or sphingolipid levels fall when viability fails.
directions.prior_work: PMID 35649364 links Fur loss and the sphingolipid CPG to lipid A dispensability, and PMID 19520766 and PMID 30210482 define the Fur regulon. None tests the respiratory operon as a requirement for the rescue.
directions.question: Caulobacter tolerates lipid A loss without Fur and with sphingolipids, yet sphingolipid synthesis genes were not induced. A respiratory operon (cbb3, cyd, fix) raised by Fur loss stayed at normal transcript levels in a strain lacking a stress regulator, in rich medium only. Is that operon needed for rescue?
directions.readiness_basis: Strain construction and lipidomics are new experiments; only a supporting fitness check uses catalog data, and that data holds no iron-limitation conditions.
directions.test: In the Caulobacter lipid A-loss strain with Fur deleted and the buffering gene deleted, delete the cbb3 respiratory operon and score viability, with the Fur-deleted background alone as a comparison. Because the original transcript measurements were made only in routine rich medium, test viability and respiration also at low oxygen and under iron limitation. Measure sphingolipid levels by lipidomics. Check whether the same operon genes show fitness effects in the Caulobacter transposon-fitness data, which holds no iron-limitation conditions.
directions.title: Might buffered respiratory genes, not sphingolipid induction, carry Caulobacter's tolerance of lipid A loss?
directions.why_it_matters: It would redirect the explanation of outer-membrane rescue from lipid substitution toward cellular energetics, and reveal which respiratory conditions a lipid A-free envelope needs. If the operon proves dispensable, the buffering is a side effect with no role in rescue.

directions.hypothesis: Condition-class conservation of unannotated gene families extends across phyla. Orthologs of the same family in Proteobacteria and in Bacteroides or Methanococcus have specific phenotypes in the same condition class more often than expected from how common each class is.
directions.outcomes: Support: cross-phylum pairs agree on condition class clearly more often than shuffled pairs, though less than within Proteobacteria. Refute: agreement across phyla is no better than shuffled labels, which would mean phenotype class is not a conserved property of dark families at this depth.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 29769716 and 22125499 assign condition-specific phenotypes to poorly annotated genes within single organisms, but neither asks whether the phenotype class is conserved between distant lineages.
directions.question: Over half of the unannotated gene families are pan-bacterial. When such a family has a measured phenotype in one distant lineage, does its ortholog in another lineage show the same kind of condition-specific phenotype (stress, carbon, nitrogen, and so on)?
directions.readiness_basis: The ortholog, specific-phenotype, condition-group and gene tables are listed, but the matching and shuffling analysis has to be built.
directions.test: Take unannotated Fitness Browser genes with a strong condition-specific phenotype. Group them into ortholog sets spanning Proteobacteria and at least one non-Proteobacterial organism (Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, the two Methanococcus strains). Record each gene's dominant condition class from the specific-phenotype and condition-group tables. Compare class agreement between cross-phylum ortholog pairs with agreement after shuffling class labels among genes within each organism. A within-Proteobacteria comparison gives the upper bound.
directions.title: Do conserved unannotated genes keep their phenotype type across deeply divergent bacteria?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, a phenotype measured in a convenient Proteobacterium can guide function discovery for conserved dark genes in organisms with no mutant library. If false, phenotype transfer works only among close relatives and the pan-bacterial dark families need testing in each host.

directions.hypothesis: Essential non-core genes in ribosome and DNA-replication functions are found mostly in genomes that lack a core paralog of the same function. Those in secretion and plasmid functions sit next to mobile-element markers instead.
directions.outcomes: Support: replication and ribosome-type essential non-core genes show mutually exclusive presence with a core paralog, and the plasmid-type ones sit by mobile-element genes. Refute: they co-occur with a core paralog as often as other genes, or have no mobile-element association.
directions.prior_work: PMID 33760724 links essential genes outside the core to mobile elements in Xanthomonas, and PMID 36097170 shows strain-dependent essentiality in S. pneumoniae. Neither tests whether the non-core essential genes substitute for a missing core paralog.
directions.question: Many essential genes are not in the core genome, and they are enriched in ribosome, DNA replication, type 4 secretion and plasmid replication functions. Are these strain-specific replacements that matter only where the core copy is absent, or are they mobile-element addiction genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene, annotation, cluster and genome tables are listed, but the catalog match did not show the table linking individual genes to clusters or the Fitness Browser-to-pangenome link that the paralog search needs.
directions.test: For the essential non-core genes in the Fitness Browser organisms, assign functions from the SEED annotations. Using the pangenome gene-cluster and genome tables, plus the table linking genes to their clusters, ask for each gene whether genomes of the same species lacking it carry a core paralog with the same function. Separately, test whether the secretion and plasmid genes lie within a few genes of transposase, integrase or phage genes. Compare with matched non-essential non-core genes. Exclude clades with very few genomes, where core status is trivially high.
directions.title: Are essential genes outside the core genome stand-ins for missing core machinery?
directions.why_it_matters: The first outcome would show that essentiality can be reassigned between lineages by genome context. The second would show that part of apparent essentiality is dependence on selfish elements. Each changes how essential-gene lists are used as drug-target or minimal-genome catalogues.

directions.hypothesis: Bioleaching genera are enriched for a small set of specific metal-handling gene families (for example particular efflux or arsenic and copper resistance families) even though their total metal-gene count is unremarkable.
directions.outcomes: Support: a few named families are clearly more frequent in bioleachers than in size-matched background, and are core to the genus. Refute: no individual family differs from the matched background, so the lack of a group-level signal holds at family resolution.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 30389769 and 12829273 describe metal-resistance genes in Acidithiobacillus and widespread basic defences, and 29150517 covers Leptospirillum, but none compares specialists with a genome-size-matched background family by family.
directions.question: After correcting for genome size, bioleaching genera as a group do not carry more metal-signature genes than other bacteria, yet one genus, Leptospirillum, scores high individually. Do these specialists differ in which metal families they carry?
directions.readiness_basis: Annotation, cluster and genome-size tables cover all 27,702 pangenomes; the matched family-level comparison has to be computed.
directions.test: Using the pangenome gene clusters with their ortholog (KO) annotations across all species, compare each bioleaching genus (Acidithiobacillus, Leptospirillum and other named bioleachers) with background species matched on genome size and phylum. Test family by family for enrichment among the metal-signature KOs, and check whether any enriched family is in the core or accessory genome of the genus.
directions.title: Do bioleaching bacteria carry different metal-resistance families rather than more of them?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, metal tolerance in extreme acidic habitats comes from selected families, and a summed signature score hides it. If false, specialist metal lifestyles need no special gene content and the explanation must lie in regulation or expression.

directions.hypothesis: Members of accessory-dominated modules lie close together on the chromosome and are present or absent together across genomes of a species far more than members of core modules.
directions.outcomes: Support: accessory modules are more compact and show stronger joint presence and absence across genomes than core modules, often with mobile-element neighbours. Refute: they are as dispersed and as independently distributed as core modules.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 38948139 and 42262111 report core enrichment of fitness genes and co-expression modules in single species. Neither asks whether accessory modules are physically and evolutionarily coherent units.
directions.question: Some co-regulated fitness modules are made mostly of accessory genes. Are these modules physically clustered operons that are gained and lost together, as horizontally transferred units would be, or are they niche-specific modules that simply sit in variable parts of the genome?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene coordinates, cluster and genome tables are listed; the module membership lists come from the project's own outputs and the gene-to-cluster membership table was not among the catalog-matched tables.
directions.test: Take modules with under half core genes and core-dominated modules from the Fitness Browser organisms with pangenome links. For each module, measure the chromosomal span of its members from gene coordinates, and measure how often members co-occur across the species' genomes using the pangenome cluster and genome tables together with the table linking genes to clusters. Check whether members have mobile-element annotations. Compare accessory with core modules, controlling for module size.
directions.title: Do accessory fitness modules move between genomes as intact transferable units?
directions.why_it_matters: Support would show that horizontal transfer of whole functional units, not single genes, shapes the variable genome. Refutation would send attention to niche-specific regulation of scattered genes.

directions.hypothesis: The shared genes are important under non-ionic osmotic stress (such as sorbitol or sucrose) about as often as under sodium chloride, and less often under potassium or choline chloride at matched strength.
directions.outcomes: Support: shared genes are as often important under non-ionic osmolytes as under sodium chloride. Refute: they are important under sodium chloride but not under matched osmolytes, or the experiments needed do not exist in enough organisms.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 32986214 and 19227837 study copper, zinc and nickel effects in other systems and do not dissect a genome-wide gene set shared between metal and osmotic stress.
directions.question: About four in ten metal-important genes are also important under salt stress, and chloride delivery does not explain it (zinc sulfate overlapped as much as chloride metals). Is the shared set a general osmotic or envelope response, or specific to sodium?
directions.readiness_basis: The condition fields are listed, but the catalog did not show whether enough potassium chloride, choline chloride and non-ionic osmolyte experiments exist across organisms.
directions.test: In Fitness Browser organisms with several salt and osmolyte experiments, select the metal-important genes that are also important under sodium chloride. Using the experiment table's condition fields, find experiments with potassium chloride, choline chloride, sorbitol or sucrose. Measure what fraction of the shared set is important in each, relative to the fraction of other genes. Check that the answer is not dominated by one organism, such as Synechococcus elongatus.
directions.title: Is the shared metal and salt gene set an osmotic response rather than a sodium one?
directions.why_it_matters: This would show what the shared metal-salt gene set is and how to correct for it in metal studies. Support points to envelope and osmotic biology. Refutation points to sodium-specific handling or to metal-specific mechanisms.

directions.hypothesis: Knockout-essential genes that the transposon screen calls dispensable have insertions concentrated near the 3' end or between domains, and truncated versions of such genes support growth when constructed directly.
directions.outcomes: Support: insertions cluster in tolerated tail regions and the truncation alleles are viable. Refute: insertions are spread through the gene, or truncations that remove the same region are lethal, so the discordance has another cause.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18319726 built the complete ADP1 deletion collection and PMID 25968644 introduced barcoded transposon fitness. Neither tests whether partial gene products explain disagreement between the two assays.
directions.question: Transposon-based essentiality calls in Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 agree poorly with complete-knockout calls in rich medium, with low recall and precision. Do insertions in knockout-essential genes leave partly working proteins?
directions.readiness_basis: Insertion positions are not shown in the catalog, and viability of truncation alleles requires new strain construction.
directions.test: For ADP1, take genes that complete knockouts show to be essential in rich medium but that the transposon screen calls dispensable. Map their insertion positions relative to domain boundaries. Then build C-terminal truncations or domain-deletion alleles for a sample of them, with full-gene deletions as controls, and measure growth in the same rich medium.
directions.title: Do transposon insertions miss essential genes because truncated proteins keep function?
directions.why_it_matters: Support would show that insertion-based essentiality maps under-call essentials that tolerate truncation, and would mark the domains needed for viability. Refutation would push explanations toward condition differences or insertion-mapping error.

directions.hypothesis: Accessory genes whose annotation names a specific substrate or stress show phenotypes as often as core genes when that condition was tested. Their apparent neutrality comes from conditions never offered.
directions.outcomes: Support: accessory genes with a tested cognate condition show phenotypes at core-like rates, and new screens reveal phenotypes for many untested ones. Refute: accessory genes stay neutral even under their predicted substrate, so they are inert in the laboratory.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29769716 reports condition-specific phenotypes for poorly annotated genes, and PMID 38948139 finds fitness genes enriched in core genes. Neither tests whether missing matching conditions explain accessory genes' apparent neutrality.
directions.question: Genes with condition-specific phenotypes are more often core than accessory, contrary to the idea that condition-specific means niche-specific. Is that because the conditions that would reveal accessory genes' functions are missing from laboratory panels?
directions.readiness_basis: Experiment, annotation, specific-phenotype and cluster tables are in the catalog. The core-status link and the substrate mapping must be built, and the follow-up screens need new measurements.
directions.test: Annotate genes in the transposon-mutant fitness collection with the substrate or stress implied by their SEED role or domain. For each organism, check from the experiment table whether that condition was tested. Link genes to core or accessory status through the pangenome gene clusters. Compare phenotype rates for core and accessory genes separately for tested and untested cognate conditions, using the specific-phenotype table. For organisms with many untested cases, run new fitness screens adding the missing substrates and ask whether previously neutral accessory genes gain phenotypes.
directions.title: Do accessory genes look condition-neutral because labs never offer their substrate?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, the core enrichment is a sampling artifact of the laboratory panel, and accessory genes are as condition-dependent as core genes. It would also give a way to choose conditions that expose unmeasured accessory function.

directions.hypothesis: Core resistance genes are more often tagged with condition-specific phenotypes under non-antibiotic stresses (metals, salt, nutrient limitation) than accessory resistance genes. This holds within each mechanism class, and under both keyword-derived and ontology-derived mechanism labels, so conservation reflects a second physiological role rather than resistance.
directions.outcomes: Support: core resistance genes have more non-antibiotic condition-specific phenotypes than accessory ones within every mechanism class, under both labelling schemes. Refute: no difference within classes, so the mechanism-conservation link comes from class composition alone. A pattern present only under keyword labels and absent under ontology labels is treated as unsupported.
directions.prior_work: PMID 25861385 and PMID 26203082 address the cost of resistance but not why resistance genes are conserved; PMID 29769716 reports condition-specific mutant phenotypes without relating them to resistance-gene conservation.
directions.question: Resistance mechanism predicts whether a resistance gene is conserved across a species, yet not the growth cost of disrupting it. Are intrinsic efflux pumps and beta-lactamases kept in the core genome for everyday roles under non-antibiotic stress? The mechanism labels behind the conservation result came from keyword matching on product descriptions, not the CARD Antibiotic Resistance Ontology.
directions.readiness_basis: The fitness and pangenome tables are in the catalog, but the table linking fitness-browser genes to pangenome clusters was not shown and may need to be rebuilt; the ontology remapping must be derived from product descriptions.
directions.test: Link resistance-gene calls in the pangenome to mutant-fitness genes in the 25 bacteria used for the cost comparison. Take mechanism labels from keyword matching on product descriptions, as the earlier work did, and repeat with labels remapped to the CARD Antibiotic Resistance Ontology to see whether the result depends on the labelling. Split genes into core and accessory within each mechanism class (efflux, enzymatic inactivation, metal resistance). Count, per gene, the non-antibiotic experiments with a condition-specific phenotype, then compare core with accessory within each class. Repeat per organism so one species is not driving the pattern. Most of these species have few genomes (median 9), so the core label is imprecise.
directions.title: Do conserved resistance genes persist because they serve non-antibiotic physiology rather than resistance?
directions.why_it_matters: If it holds, the conserved fraction of the resistome partly reflects ordinary physiology, and counts of core resistance genes overstate resistance risk. If it fails, conservation by mechanism is better explained by inheritance history and mobility, or by how the classes were labelled.

directions.hypothesis: Costly dispensable genes occur in contiguous runs on the chromosome whose members share the same fitness gains when deleted, and removing a whole run restores more growth than removing any single member. A few element-level burdens, such as prophage activity, then account for most of the class.
directions.outcomes: Clustering and correlated fitness in step 1 support only the spatial part of the idea. The element-level mechanism is supported only if deleting the whole element gives a growth gain larger than the sum of single-gene deletions, or if one element-wide function (such as induced prophage activity) accounts for it. Refute: costly genes are scattered like random genes, or runs form but whole-element deletion gives no more gain than single-gene deletions.
directions.prior_work: PMID 22448042 predicts that costly, dispensable functions are lost and PMID 30809245 describes prophage remnants as innovation hotspots, but neither measures whether the burden is concentrated in contiguous islands or tests whole-element against single-gene removal.
directions.question: Costly but dispensable genes are strongly enriched for transposase, integrase and prophage keywords, and Pseudomonas stutzeri RCH2 stands out with 21.5% of its genes in this class. Does the cost come from entire inserted elements acting as units, or from individual genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene coordinates, annotations and experiments are in the catalog, but the per-gene fitness table was not shown and must be assembled from per-organism tables; the deletion step needs new measurements.
directions.test: Step 1, lakehouse analysis: in P. stutzeri RCH2 and Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron (14.0% costly dispensable), place costly dispensable genes on the chromosome using gene coordinates. Test whether they cluster into runs more than a shuffled placement of equally many genes predicts, whether neighbours within a run show correlated fitness across experiments, and whether runs carry mobile-element annotation. Use a conserved costly set as a control. Step 2, experiment: for one or two runs in RCH2 that pass step 1, delete the whole element and, separately, its individual member genes, and compare growth gains in the laboratory media where the genes were costly.
directions.title: Is the cost of dispensable genes carried by whole mobile islands rather than single genes?
directions.why_it_matters: If whole elements carry the burden, loss of costly genes is a matter of losing intact islands, and the cost is not a property of individual genes. It would also explain why such genes are rare in other genomes and why one strain can be an extreme outlier. If runs form but no element-level burden appears, the cost lies in the individual genes.

directions.hypothesis: In species from diverse environments, accessory resistance genes sit next to mobile-element genes more often than in narrow-niche species with matched genome counts. Heavy sampling alone would not produce this difference.
directions.outcomes: Support: mobile flanking of accessory resistance genes rises with environmental diversity after stratifying, and exceeds the control genes. Refute: flanking is similar across diversity levels, or rises equally for control genes. A result seen only in the metadata-rich subset would be treated as inconclusive for the wider collection.
directions.prior_work: PMID 36882798 shows latent resistance genes are mobile across microbiomes, and PMID 38457973 links environmental drivers to resistance accumulation; neither tests mobile context across species in relation to environmental diversity.
directions.question: Species from more varied environments carry more resistance genes, and a smaller share of them are core. Is this because such species acquire resistance by horizontal transfer, or just because they have been sampled more heavily?
directions.readiness_basis: Resistance calls, annotations and embeddings are in the catalog; neighbour assignment must be derived and may be incomplete in fragmented assemblies, and embeddings cover only part of the genomes.
directions.test: Take species with at least 3 genomes and environmental embeddings. Only 28% of genomes have these embeddings, and they are biased toward genomes with geographic metadata, so first compare the embedded subset with the rest on taxonomy and genome count, and repeat the main comparison within phyla to limit that bias. Use the contig-and-index structure of resistance gene cluster identifiers to find neighbouring genes, and score neighbours for transposase, integrase and phage annotations. Compare the share of mobile-flanked accessory resistance genes between high- and low-diversity species, stratified by genome count and phylum, and test the same in matched non-resistance accessory genes as a control.
directions.title: Do species from diverse environments gain resistance genes through mobile elements?
directions.why_it_matters: It would point to horizontal transfer as the route by which environmental breadth accumulates resistance, which affects where surveillance should focus. If not, the correlation is a sampling artefact.

directions.hypothesis: Lanmodulin was gained in a few ancestral lineages and then lost repeatedly. Carriers without xoxF keep it for lanthanide buffering or storage, so its presence is not tied to the dehydrogenase.
directions.outcomes: Support: few gains followed by repeated losses, neighbouring genes unrelated to methanol oxidation in carriers lacking xoxF, and a deletion effect on lanthanide handling. Refute: lanmodulin always sits beside xoxF-linked genes, or its deletion has no effect without xoxF.
directions.prior_work: PMIDs 30351021 and 35814700 characterize lanmodulin in Methylobacterium and PMID 34737731 compares Methylobacterium genomes. None traces gain and loss of lanmodulin or tests its role where xoxF is absent.
directions.question: Why is lanmodulin confined to three alpha-Proteobacterial methylotroph families, and what does it do in the genomes that carry it without the lanthanide-dependent methanol enzyme?
directions.readiness_basis: Annotation, gene-to-cluster and taxonomy tables are in the catalog, but a gene tree and neighbourhood analysis must be built, and gene position columns were not shown by the catalog.
directions.test: Build a gene tree of lanmodulin across the genomes that carry a validated copy (62 genomes from 10 species, all within Beijerinckiaceae, Acetobacteraceae or Hyphomicrobiaceae) and compare it with the species tree to count gains and losses. Compare the genes next to lanmodulin in genomes with and without xoxF (xoxF co-occurred in 49 of the 62). Then grow a lanmodulin-carrying strain that lacks xoxF in metal-limited medium with and without lanthanum, comparing wild type with a lanmodulin deletion for lanthanide uptake and survival.
directions.title: Is lanmodulin an ancient methylotroph-lineage tool or a lanthanide store used without xoxF?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate a lanthanide-handling protein from the enzyme it was assumed to serve. Lanmodulin presence could then not be used to predict lanthanide-dependent metabolism, and engineered lanmodulin variants would not mimic a natural role.

directions.hypothesis: Within Acidobacteriota, xoxF carriage rises with soil acidity and falls in neutral or alkaline soils. The same pattern holds inside other xoxF-carrying phyla, so habitat chemistry rather than taxonomy drives it.
directions.outcomes: Support: carriage rises as pH falls within genus, in several phyla, and not for the calcium-dependent enzyme. Refute: no pH relationship within genus, or the enrichment is explained by a few soil-specific genera.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38369453 reports xoxF clusters in Acidobacteria in weathered granite and soil but does not test a habitat variable within one phylum. PMID 32341564 supplies the taxonomy used to stratify.
directions.question: Is the soil and sediment enrichment of xoxF that persists inside Acidobacteriota driven by chemistry that makes lanthanides available, such as lower pH?
directions.readiness_basis: Genome, annotation and biosample attribute tables are listed, but the catalog did not show whether soil pH is recorded for enough genomes.
directions.test: Link Acidobacteriota genomes, and genomes from other xoxF-carrying phyla, to sample metadata for soil pH, soil type and depth. Model xoxF carriage against pH while holding genus fixed, in isolate genomes and in soil metagenome-assembled genomes separately. Repeat in the other phyla. Add a prediction that could fail: the relationship should be absent for the calcium-dependent methanol enzyme, which does not need lanthanides.
directions.title: Does soil acidity, which frees lanthanides, explain xoxF enrichment within Acidobacteriota?
directions.why_it_matters: It would give a mechanism for the soil signal that survived a within-phylum comparison, and would let soil pH predict where lanthanide-dependent methylotrophy matters.

directions.hypothesis: Metagenome-assembled xoxF carriers without PQQ synthesis come from samples that contain PQQ-synthesizing community members more often than matched carriers with PQQ synthesis do, and this is not explained by low assembly completeness.
directions.outcomes: Support: PQQ-lacking carriers sit in PQQ-producer-rich samples beyond completeness-matched controls, and spent medium restores growth. Refute: the pattern disappears after completeness control, or the isolate grows without help.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29997591 and PMID 24816778 describe lanthanide-dependent enzymes and their distribution among methylotrophs. None asks whether carriers without cofactor synthesis rely on community supply.
directions.question: Do xoxF-carrying genomes with no pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) synthesis genes in either annotation source live alongside PQQ producers, consistent with cofactor sharing?
directions.readiness_basis: Catalogs of metagenome-assembled genomes with completeness and sample ids plus annotation tables are listed, but the catalog did not show whether gene-level calls exist for the metagenome-assembled genomes.
directions.test: Take xoxF carriers with no PQQ evidence from either annotation source and find those that are metagenome-assembled genomes with sample context. Compare the share of PQQ-carrying genomes in the same sample against matched xoxF carriers that do have PQQ synthesis, controlling for completeness and contamination. Then test whether spent medium from a PQQ-producing methylotroph restores lanthanide-dependent growth of an isolate lacking PQQ synthesis.
directions.title: Do xoxF carriers without their own PQQ synthesis depend on neighbours for the cofactor?
directions.why_it_matters: It would reveal a cofactor dependency in methylotroph communities. Otherwise these genomes reflect assembly gaps or lost genes, which would change how the xoxF census is read.

directions.hypothesis: Outside known methylotroph families, most xoxF carriers lack the downstream genes for formaldehyde and formate oxidation, so xoxF abundance reflects general alcohol oxidation rather than methylotrophy.
directions.outcomes: Support: most carriers outside methylotroph families lack downstream genes, and isolates oxidize other alcohols lanthanide-dependently but not methanol. Refute: downstream pathway genes are present in most carriers, and isolates grow on methanol with lanthanum.
directions.prior_work: PMID 41636527 and PMID 42678158 explore wider methylotrophic metabolism and xoxF signals in wetlands, and PMID 41023737 covers methane oxidizers. None tests whether xoxF carriers across a large genome set carry full methylotrophy pathways.
directions.question: In xoxF-carrying genomes outside classic methylotroph families, is the enzyme part of a methanol-oxidation pathway or a broader alcohol and aldehyde oxidizer?
directions.readiness_basis: Both annotation sources and taxonomy for the full genome collection are listed, and the pathway scoring must be built from them.
directions.test: For every xoxF carrier in the 293,059-genome collection, score methylotrophy support: partner periplasmic genes, formaldehyde and formate oxidation, and C1 assimilation. Summarize by family and compare known methylotroph families with the rest, reporting each annotation source separately because they disagree for some markers. Then test growth on methanol and on other alcohols with and without lanthanum for a few non-methylotroph carriers, for example in Acidobacteriota.
directions.title: Is xoxF in non-methylotrophs a methanol enzyme or a general alcohol oxidizer?
directions.why_it_matters: The large lead of xoxF over the calcium-dependent enzyme is usually read as lanthanide-based methylotrophy dominating. If most carriers are not methylotrophs, that reading and the estimate of how common lanthanide-dependent methanol oxidation is would both change.

directions.hypothesis: Adding free leucine or arginine to soil lowers the community's synthesis gene content for that amino acid over time, relative to unamended and glucose-amended soil. The natural-sample association is a single-study correlation and should be read as a lead only.
directions.outcomes: Support: amino acid amendment lowers synthesis gene content for the added amino acid relative to both controls, and the negative association also appears in at least one further study. Refute: amendment changes nothing, or the association vanishes when taxonomic composition is accounted for.
directions.prior_work: PMID 37322284 and PMID 35592760 study provisioning and cross-feeding of amino acid auxotrophs in cultures, and PMID 31316056 and PMID 35085485 predict metabolites from community sequences. None tests, in natural samples or in an amendment, whether free amino acids drive loss of synthesis genes.
directions.question: In soil communities, is the lower leucine and arginine synthesis capacity seen where those amino acids are abundant caused by gene loss driven by free amino acids, or by some other factor such as which community members are present?
directions.readiness_basis: Metabolite intensities, sample-to-study links, community taxonomy and genome pathway scores are in the catalog, but the taxonomy-to-genome mapping and per-sample completeness must be computed; the catalog did not show how many studies have paired data, and the amendment needs new measurements.
directions.test: Step 1 (lakehouse): in the soil samples with untargeted metabolite data, estimate each community's synthesis completeness for leucine and arginine by combining its taxonomic profile with genome-level pathway scores for the matched species. Relate this to the measured amino acid signal within the dominant study, and look for any other study with paired metabolite and sequence data to see whether the direction repeats. Use tyrosine, which showed an opposite weak association, and isoleucine, which showed none, as pathways where no negative association is expected. Step 2 (experiment): add leucine or arginine to soil microcosms and follow synthesis gene content by shotgun sequencing, against unamended and glucose-amended controls.
directions.title: Do soil microbes lose amino-acid synthesis genes where free amino acids are plentiful?
directions.why_it_matters: A cause-and-effect link would show that dependence on shared metabolites arises inside natural communities, not only in two-species cultures. The present evidence is a correlation in which nearly all samples, and all leucine samples, come from one soil study, so it cannot say which variable moves first or whether it holds elsewhere.

directions.hypothesis: Among species with many genomes, the count of metabolic ecotypes rises with the breadth of environments the genomes were drawn from. Phylogenetic grouping alone does not account for this.
directions.outcomes: Support: breadth predicts ecotype count within families after covariates. Refute: the relation disappears within families or tracks only genome count, which would mean ecotypes mostly reflect sampling and lineage.
directions.prior_work: PMID 24465487 links metabolic flexibility to spatial distribution of communities, and PMID 22928415 maps soil niche space with taxonomy and traits. Neither relates within-species metabolic ecotype counts to environmental breadth across thousands of species.
directions.question: Do species that split into more metabolic ecotypes occupy a wider range of environments than species with few ecotypes, beyond what the number of sequenced genomes and the pangenome's openness explain?
directions.readiness_basis: Pathway scores, genome-to-species links and environment text are in the catalog; the ecotype clustering and embedding-based breadth must be computed, with embedding coverage limited.
directions.test: For the species with at least 50 genomes and several variable pathways, cluster genomes by pathway presence to count ecotypes. Measure environmental breadth as the spread of satellite-derived environmental embeddings per species, and as the number of distinct isolation-source categories. Model ecotype count against breadth with genome count, openness and genus as covariates. Keep only species whose genomes have embeddings (about 28% of genomes), and repeat the analysis within each family.
directions.title: Do species with more metabolic ecotypes live across a wider range of environments?
directions.why_it_matters: Variable pathways track pangenome openness, but phylogeny dominates gene content in most species, so an ecological explanation is unproven. A link to environmental breadth would show that metabolic ecotypes are habitat adaptation rather than lineage structure.

directions.hypothesis: Most genes needed specifically for urea growth lie outside the urease cluster, including transport and regulatory genes, and they are less conserved across Acinetobacter than genes needed on other carbon sources.
directions.outcomes: Support: several top urea-specific genes are non-urease and are more often variable across genomes than genes specific to other sources, and deletions impair urea growth. Refute: the urea-specific set is just urease and its accessory genes, or the profile is no more distinct than for the other carbon sources once noise is accounted for.
directions.prior_work: PMID 18319726 built the single-gene deletion collection for ADP1 but did not ask which genes are specific to urea.
directions.question: What genes make up the largely separate fitness profile for urea in Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1, and are they beyond the urease and nickel-handling genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Pangenome and BacDive tables are in the catalog, but the ADP1 growth matrix is not among the tables shown, so its location in the lakehouse is unconfirmed.
directions.test: Step 1: from the ADP1 mutant growth data across eight carbon sources, rank genes by how much more their effect on urea differs from the other conditions, and check how many fall outside urease and nickel genes. Step 2: place those genes in the Acinetobacter pangenome and compare their conservation with genes specific to quinate or other carbon sources. Compare with BacDive urea-use calls for Acinetobacter strains. Step 3: delete the top non-urease candidates and measure growth on urea.
directions.title: Does urea use in Acinetobacter depend on genes outside the classical urease cluster?
directions.why_it_matters: Urea fitness was nearly unrelated to fitness on other carbon sources. That fits a separate gene set, but the genes have not been named. Identifying them would show whether nitrogen-source use is a lineage-variable trait.

directions.hypothesis: For these reactions, fitness-supported candidate genes encode enzymes whose annotated reactions are chemically more similar to the gapfilled reaction than random genes from the same organism are.
directions.outcomes: Support: candidate enzymes are more similar to the gapfilled reaction than random genes, and some candidates turn the substrate over in assays. Refute: similarity is indistinguishable from random and assays are negative, pointing to unknown families.
directions.prior_work: PMID 30910961 annotates orphan and novel reactions from substrate reactive sites, and PMID 25968644 provides the fitness method. Neither tests whether fitness-linked candidates for specific unresolved gapfilled reactions are promiscuous known enzymes.
directions.question: Do gapfilled reactions that have no enzyme number, and that are rarely resolved to a gene, reflect known enzymes acting on non-native substrates rather than undiscovered enzyme families?
directions.readiness_basis: Reactions, fitness and annotation tables are in the catalog; the gapfilled reaction list and the similarity scoring between candidate and gapfilled reactions must be rebuilt and computed.
directions.test: For each gapfilled reaction without an enzyme number, collect genes whose mutants show fitness effects on the carbon source that required the reaction, across the Fitness Browser organisms. Take each candidate's annotated reaction from its best-hit pathway and functional annotations, and score chemical similarity to the gapfilled reaction by comparing substrates, products and reaction definitions from the biochemistry reaction table (similarity is computed here, as the catalog did not show a precomputed similarity table among the tables listed). Compare with matched-count random genes and with reactions that have enzyme numbers. Test top candidates with purified-protein assays on the predicted substrate.
directions.title: Are gapfilled reactions without enzyme numbers done by known enzymes with broad substrate range?
directions.why_it_matters: Of the 50 reactions without enzyme numbers, only 8 were resolved, against 88 of 151 for reactions with them. If promiscuity explains the gap, model repair should search known enzymes broadly. If not, truly new families are probably needed.

directions.hypothesis: D. vulgaris grows without serine by making it from glycine or threonine, so mutants of the glycine-to-serine enzyme lose fitness in serine-free defined medium while homologs of the canonical phosphoglycerate route have little effect.
directions.outcomes: Support: growth without serine, and strong fitness loss of the glycine-route gene only in serine-free medium. Refute: no growth without serine, which would confirm auxotrophy, or growth with no fitness effect in any candidate, which would point to an unannotated route.
directions.prior_work: PMID 29324779 fills predicted amino acid pathway gaps with high-throughput genetics and covers D. vulgaris, and PMID 15077118 is its genome. Neither says whether this organism has a serine gap or how it would be bridged.
directions.question: Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough is the only one of seven organisms predicted to lack complete serine synthesis. Does it make serine by a non-canonical route, and which genes carry it?
directions.readiness_basis: The decisive test needs serine-free growth and labeled-glycine tracing, which are new measurements; fitness and annotation tables for this organism are in the catalog, but whether serine-free defined-medium experiments exist was not shown.
directions.test: From mutant fitness data for D. vulgaris in defined media with and without serine or glycine, compare fitness of glycine hydroxymethyltransferase, threonine aldolase and phosphoglycerate-route homologs, and list any genes with strong serine-dependent effects. Then grow the wild type in serine-free defined medium, with labeled glycine to trace serine formation, and complement top candidate genes.
directions.title: Does Desulfovibrio vulgaris make serine by a route that pathway predictors miss?
directions.why_it_matters: A true serine requirement would be an unusual auxotrophy for a free-living sulfate reducer. A hidden route would show a systematic blind spot of automated pathway prediction in anaerobes.

directions.hypothesis: Acidity is the primary driver. In samples matched for pH, the abundance contrast between the two clusters largely disappears, whereas in samples matched for temperature it persists. In culture, strains of the first cluster outgrow strains of the second at low pH at both temperatures.
directions.outcomes: Support: the contrast between clusters shrinks to little in pH-matched samples but persists in temperature-matched ones, and acid-cluster strains win at low pH at both temperatures. Refutation: the contrast persists after pH matching, or temperature alone changes which strain wins in culture.
directions.prior_work: PMID 38366921 and PMID 40118314 tie pH and temperature to Ralstonia and Sphingomonas only in fish skin and acid mine drainage; none separates the two drivers for these two clusters worldwide.
directions.question: Two groups of genera found at Oak Ridge (Rhodanobacter, Ralstonia and Dyella versus Brevundimonas, Caulobacter and Sphingomonas) occupy different habitats worldwide. The first group lives in environments 1.35 pH units more acidic and 6.9°C warmer. Which of the two variables actually drives the split?
directions.readiness_basis: The survey analysis can use global OTU counts with matched soil pH and temperature columns shown in the catalog, but the decisive growth experiment across pH and temperature needs new measurements.
directions.test: Step 1 (lakehouse): join global amplicon survey counts for the six genera to the soil pH and air temperature layers attached to each sample. Compare the abundance contrast between the two clusters in pH-matched samples that differ in temperature, and in temperature-matched samples that differ in pH. Only samples with these layers can be used. Step 2 (experiment): grow strains of Dyella, Ralstonia, Sphingomonas and Caulobacter from the mutant fitness collection across a pH gradient at two temperatures, each alone and in mixed culture.
directions.title: Is acidity, rather than temperature, what separates two Oak Ridge genus clusters worldwide?
directions.why_it_matters: A global niche partition only helps predict which lab strains stand in for field organisms if its driver is known. Naming pH rather than temperature would also show which Oak Ridge contamination variable to prioritise. The original observation reports shared or exclusive niches, not direct interaction, so this separates habitat filtering from correlation.

directions.hypothesis: The separation is stronger than shared ancestry predicts, because carrying both kinds of capacity creates a redox or regulatory conflict. Isolates that carry both should therefore use an aromatic compound more slowly or less fully when a non-aromatic carbon source is present.
directions.outcomes: Support: co-occurrence is lower than the within-genus shuffles give and aromatic use is delayed or reduced when the second carbon source is present. Refutation: co-occurrence matches the within-genus shuffles and mixed-substrate growth is simply the sum of the two single-substrate results.
directions.prior_work: PMID 22026719 finds aromatic versatility in Burkholderiales to be a lineage-level property shaped by habitat; it does not test whether aromatic and non-aromatic capacities exclude each other beyond lineage expectation.
directions.question: Only 25 of 3109 genomes carry both an aromatic and a non-aromatic capacity from the carbon census, and the few genomes with three or more capacities concentrate in Paraburkholderia, Burkholderia and Hydrogenophaga. Is this separation a metabolic or regulatory conflict, or simply lineage history?
directions.readiness_basis: The decisive mixed-substrate growth tests need new measurements; for the shuffle, the catalog shows only per-isolate orthologous-group presence, and the 3109-genome capacity matrix and its gene-to-capacity mapping were not shown, so their availability is unknown.
directions.test: Step 1: build a lineage-aware expectation by shuffling capacity calls among genomes within the same genus, and ask whether the observed number of genomes carrying both kinds is lower than the shuffled genomes give. Use the census capacity calls as defined (eight aromatic/alkaloid capacities); the xanthine call that was mis-scored as carbon catabolism must be excluded, since the committed tables predate its removal. Step 2: grow versatile Paraburkholderia and Hydrogenophaga isolates on an aromatic compound alone, a non-aromatic census compound alone, and both together, recording growth timing and the NADH/NAD+ balance.
directions.title: Do aromatic and non-aromatic catabolic capacities avoid each other beyond what lineage predicts?
directions.why_it_matters: A real conflict would explain why specialists dominate and would make aromatic-degrading chassis for bioremediation hard to combine with broad carbon use. If lineage alone explains it, versatility is limited by evolutionary history, not by physiology.

directions.hypothesis: Across samples within the same study, the signal of compounds with no utilizer call is weaker where Comamonadaceae genera are abundant than where they are scarce. At least some of these compounds are depleted by pure isolates of those genera, and carbon from the compound ends up in their cells.
directions.outcomes: Support: within a study, the compound signal drops as these genera become more abundant, isolates deplete the compound, and the isotope label appears in them. Refutation: no within-study relation, or depletion occurs only in mixed enrichments without isolate-level or isotope evidence.
directions.prior_work: PMID 32961457, PMID 36688698 and PMID 19457026 show only that related genera occur in freshwater biofilms; none links their abundance to depletion of compounds without a known degrader.
directions.question: Most census compounds, notably alkaloids and terpenoids, got no isolate utilizer call in the resources queried, though literature beyond that search may exist. Periphyton samples are rich in Comamonadaceae genera. Do isolates of these genera actually degrade such compounds?
directions.readiness_basis: The metabolomics, taxonomy and file-bridge tables are in the catalog, but compound identifiers must be matched to the census list and the catalog did not show how many samples have both data types; the isolate and isotope tests need new measurements.
directions.test: Step 1 (lakehouse): use the file-to-sample-and-study bridge to join metabolomics and taxonomic profiles to studies and ecosystem labels. Within each study, compare how strongly detectable census compounds are seen in samples rich versus poor in these genera, contrasting compounds with no utilizer call against callable ones. Compounds not detected in the metabolomics data drop out. Step 2 (experiment): grow isolates of Variovorax, Polaromonas, Hydrogenophaga and Rhizobacter individually on a few such compounds and follow compound loss. Confirm incorporation in a periphyton-inoculated enrichment by stable-isotope tracing, so depletion by another community member is ruled out.
directions.title: Do freshwater-biofilm Comamonadaceae isolates consume compounds that lack a utilizer call?
